description_ru: На саммите переводчик втайне смягчает оскорбления министров. Что случится, когда однажды он решит перевести всё слово в слово? Едкая и умная история о дипломатии.
text:
Anselm Roche had been interpreting at international summits for twenty-two years, and in that time he had committed, by his own private reckoning, roughly four thousand acts of benevolent fraud. Nobody had ever caught him, because the crime consisted entirely of making things nicer than they were. When the minister of one country said, "Your proposal is an insult to reason," Anselm would render it, in a voice like warm milk, as "My esteemed colleague's proposal raises certain interesting questions." When the other minister replied with a remark about the first minister's mother, it emerged in translation as a reflection on the importance of family values.

It was a gift, and like most gifts it had gradually become a burden. He had a small, windowless booth at the back of every conference hall, a pair of headphones that smelled of other people's ears, and the permanent sensation of being the only honest liar in the room. His wife used to say that he was the most important man at the table whom nobody had ever met. He took this, correctly, as an observation, and incorrectly, as a compliment.

The summit at Valmont was meant to settle a dispute about fishing rights in a strait so narrow that both nations could, on a clear day, hear each other's dogs. For eleven days, the delegations circled one another with the elaborate courtesy of two cats at a funeral. Minister Brandvold, tall and glacial, represented the north. Minister Okonkwo-Ferreira, round and tireless, represented the south. Neither had the slightest wish to compromise, and each was determined to be seen to wish it.

On the twelfth day, Anselm woke with a sore throat and a strange, fizzing lucidity. It was the kind of clarity that sometimes visits the very tired, the morning after a long illness, when the world seems rinsed. He drank his coffee, looked at his reflection in the kettle, and thought: what if, for one session, I simply told them what they said?

It was not a decision so much as a drift, the way a boat slips its mooring on a calm night. He took his seat in the booth. The session began. Minister Brandvold rose and delivered a speech whose gist was that the southern fishing fleet were a gang of pirates in rubber boots. Anselm took a breath, and into his microphone said, with perfect clarity, "The southern fleet are a gang of pirates in rubber boots."

The effect was extraordinary. In the hall, Minister Okonkwo-Ferreira, who had been staring at the ceiling in an attitude of sublime boredom, went rigid, then slowly purple. "Pirates?" she said, in her own language, and Anselm, in the other, said, "Pirates?" with the identical stress. He had the peculiar and slightly dizzying sensation of becoming merely a pipe.

"I wish," she continued, "to remind the honourable gentleman that his own navy has, for a decade, been run by people who could not find the sea with a map and a lantern."

"I wish to remind the honourable gentleman," Anselm told the north, in a voice of unwavering neutrality, "that his own navy has been run for a decade by people who could not find the sea with a map and a lantern."

For several seconds there was a silence of such density that one could have cut it into slices and served it with cheese. Then Minister Brandvold, to everyone's astonishment, began to laugh. It was a dry, rusty laugh, as of a gate that has not been opened since the war. "A map and a lantern," he repeated. "I have been waiting four years to be insulted in an interesting way. She is, at least, more imaginative than my cabinet."

Over the next hours, the summit achieved a velocity that diplomatic history had not witnessed since the invention of the ceasefire. The ministers, deprived of the cushioning of euphemism, discovered that insults, once delivered at face value, lost most of their power to wound. It is hard to maintain a grudge against a man who has just told you precisely what he thinks. Candour, it turned out, was a kind of solvent. By evening they had agreed on quotas, a seasonal moratorium, and a joint inspection regime. By midnight they were sharing a bottle of something clear and violent, and arguing amiably about whose grandmother made the better sausage.

Anselm sat in his booth with his headphones around his neck, feeling like a man who has accidentally defused a bomb by sneezing on it. The delegates applauded in his direction, though they did not know exactly whom they were applauding. Someone from the secretariat knocked on the glass to ask if everything was all right, because his microphone had been glowing for nine hours.

The next morning, summoned to the office of the Director of Protocol, he prepared himself for dismissal. The Director was a gaunt, courteous man with the manner of a mortician at a wedding. He laid the transcript on the desk. "Mr. Roche," he said, "I have read the record. You will appreciate that your conduct was a flagrant departure from every professional norm." "I do," said Anselm.

"It was also," continued the Director, "the only successful summit this organisation has hosted in a decade." He paused, and for the first time something that might have been a smile crossed his face, like a rumour. "Naturally, we cannot permit it to happen again. A diplomacy that depends on honesty is a diplomacy without a future. I must ask you to resume your usual standards of mendacity."

"Of course," said Anselm.

He returned to his booth the following week, put on the headphones that smelled of other people's ears, and resumed the discreet, honourable work of making everything sound nicer than it was. But on certain afternoons, when a minister said something particularly absurd, he would feel a small, warm flutter, like a coin in a pocket, and remember the day he had told the truth and the world had not ended.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Ударение на разных слогах: EU-phe-mism, mo-ra-TOR-i-um. Не переносите русские привычки.
Кончик языка слегка между зубами, воздух без голоса. Не заменяйте на с или ф.
Язык не касается нёба, губы чуть округлены. Звук мягче русского р и не раскатывается.

questions.question: What was Anselm's job?
questions.answer: He was an interpreter at international summits.

questions.question: What did Anselm usually do with insults?
questions.answer: He softened them into polite remarks.

questions.question: What happened when he translated word for word?
questions.answer: The ministers laughed and quickly reached agreements.

questions.question: What did the Director of Protocol ask him to do?
questions.answer: To resume his usual dishonesty and soften everything again.
